title: 684530587625/541NV17: The Lounge 2, St Georges Street, Tenby, SA70 7JB
text:
TRIBIWNLYS PRISIO CYMRU  -  VALUATION TRIBUNAL FOR WALES

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 1 of 8

Appellant:  Mrs Y Uka

Appeal property: The Lounge 2, St Georges Street, Tenby, SA70 7JB

Appeal number: 684530587625/541NV17

The Matter Appealed against: Non-domestic rating appeal

Date of Hearing: 19th September 2019

Appearances: Mrs Y Uka (Appellant) & Mrs S Harris (for respondent
Valuation Officer)

Date of Decision: 25th October 2019

Decision of Tribunal: Allowed in part

Members of the Tribunal: Mr J O Peake (Chairperson), Mr J Griffiths & J
Edwards

Tribunal Clerk: Mr J Evans

Reason for Decision

1. This appeal followed a proposal which sought an alteration to an entry
which appeared in the 2017 Non-Domestic Rating List. The entry in
question was described as a Café and Premises and traded under the
name “Lounge 2”. The Valuation Officer had ascribed a Rateable Value
(RV) of £17,500 which was effective from 1st April 2017.

2. On 5th March 2018, the Valuation Officer for Wales (VO) received a
proposal from Mrs Uka in which she sought a reduction in RV with effect
from 5th January 2018 due to the disruption caused by road works.

3. Since the VO had not “well-founded” the proposal, the matter was remitted
to the Valuation Tribunal for Wales as an appeal.

4. This document does not intend to be an exhaustive record of the
proceedings, but the parties can be assured that the Tribunal fully
considered all of the evidence before it arrived at its decision.
Consequently, the absence of reference to any statement, or evidence in
this record should not be construed as being overlooked.

Non-Domestic Rating Appeal

Page 2 of 8
Summary of the case

5. In her evidence, Mrs Uka gave details of the nature of the disruption
outside her premises and from when it commenced. In support of this
statement Mrs Uka presented photographs which depicted the scale of the
works. Mrs Uka did not consider that the VO had given adequate
consideration to traders who were situated in the vicinity of the works. This
was aggravated further by promises made by the local authority to ensure
that access to shops was still possible and that plant and machinery was
removed from the area at the weekends. However, the latter was not
followed up and Mrs Uka pointed out that on two occasions her business
had to close because contractors had cut through electricity cabling in the
street.

6. In her discussions with representatives of the VO, Mrs Uka said she was
told that the work would subsist for a period of 13 weeks although the
council had admitted that the same works would be completed in four.

7. Mrs Uka explained that the works had disrupted her businesses
performance in the lead up to some of her of busiest periods: The Half
Term break, Easter and May Day bank holidays. Moreover, the obstruction
caused by the works and the appeal property’s position in relation to the
“Five Arches” and public cark parks combined to exacerbate the problem.
This had a consequential affect and ensured that existing and potential
passing trade was dramatically impeded as a result of the works and all it
entailed which continued up to the Whitsun break.

8. In November 2018, the cobble street was dug up and removed to allow
Western Power to  install a three-phase power supply to the side entrance
of premises formerly used by the Nat West bank. Access from Tudor
Square into St. George’s Street was inaccessible for the duration of the
works.

9. Mrs Uka had queried with the VO why it was deemed necessary to
compare the takings of the previous year with those of the period in
dispute. She did not see the relevance for this because trading
performance might vary from year to year. Moreover, she understood that
the RV represented the open market rental value of a business which
appeared to contradict the VO’s justification for examining trading figures.
Mrs Uka acknowledged that the VO applied the same end allowance to
properties within the same proximity of the works but suggested that
greater consideration should be given to the fact that she traded as a “café
and premises”.

10. Mrs Uka said that her landlord did not suffer from the disruption caused by
the works and any loss that her business incurred as a result should be
attributed to her. She also sought an answer as to why she was given a
reduction in RV for a period of six months in respect of disruption that
lasted for six weeks in 2012-13.

Non-Domestic Rating Appeal

Page 3 of 8
11. In her conclusion, Mrs Uka referred to a tribunal hearing which took place
on 17th January 2019. At that hearing, her appeal was adjourned because
the attending VO was unable to deal with this case. Mrs Uka considered
that any financial impediment caused to her as a result of the appeal being
adjourned should be covered by the VO.

12. In response to questions, Mrs Uka confirmed that she sought a reduction
of 15% rather than the 10% the VO had conceded in the revised valuation.

13. Mrs Uka confirmed that she paid £2,083 in rates per month. Her landlord
did not reduce her rent for the duration of the disruption.

14. Mrs Uka confirmed that her business received regular customers but also
confirmed that she had lost some during the period of the works. She also
pointed out that her clientele differed from that of her neighbours.

15. In her opening remarks, Mrs Harris confirmed the capacity in which she
would present the respondent’s case.

16. In her role as advocate, Mrs Harris brought to the Tribunal’s attention the
circumstances and grounds which gave rise to the appellant making the
proposal –

“No access route from Tudor Square due to roadworks, Plant and
machinery blocking entrance to business. Operational need of the
business severely affected regarding customers and deliveries”

17. Mrs Harris explained that the statutory basis on which a rating valuation
was made was established by Paragraph 2(1) of Schedule 6 of the Local
Government Finance Act 1988, as amended. This paragraph provided the
definition of Rateable Value as was set out as follows –

The rateable value of a non-domestic hereditament … shall be taken to
be an amount equal to the rent at which it is estimated the
hereditament might reasonably be expected to let from year to year on
these three assumptions;

a. the first assumption is that the tenancy begins on the day by
reference to which the determination is to be made;

b. the second assumption is that immediately before the tenancy
begins the hereditament is in a state of reasonable repair, but
excluding from this assumption any repairs which a reasonable
landlord would consider uneconomic;

c. the third assumption is that the tenant undertakes to pay all usual
tenant’s rates and taxes and to bear the cost of the repairs and
insurance and the other expenses (if any) necessary to maintain the
hereditament in a state to command the rent mentioned above.

Non-Domestic Rating Appeal

Page 4 of 8
18. With reference to the Rating Lists (Valuation Date) (Wales) Order 2014
[the Valuation Date], Ms Harris pointed out that 1st April 2015 was the day
by reference to which the rateable values of non-domestic hereditaments
are to be determined for the purposes of the local and central non-
domestic rating lists which are compiled for Wales on 1st April 2017.

19. In considering the appellant’s case, Ms Harris had regard to the principles
established in Lotus and Delta v Culverwell (VO) [1976]; an extract of
which was referred to earlier in her submission. She said that these
principles suggested that the weight to be given to a rent depended on
how closely it complied with the statutory definition of Rateable Value.

20. In her expert witness evidence, Mrs Harris spoke to the appeal property’s
location within Tenby, its description and dimensions. The property
comprised a ground floor café with a total area of 110.35m2. In terms of
Zone A value, it had an area of 45.83m2. Mrs Harris confirmed that the
Valuation Office Agency inspected the property in March 2018.

21. In her schedule of evidence, Mrs Harris referred to a plan of Tenby which
indicated the location of the appeal and comparable properties
(“Serendipity Games” and “Cybabet”). Mrs Harris also produced
photographs of the appeal and comparable properties and referred to the
end allowances that had been granted to them as a result of the
disturbance caused by the roadworks. She presented photographs taken
from opposite ends of St Georges’ Street which reflected the works’ nature
and proximity to the subject property.

22. With regard to her two comparable properties, Mrs Harris explained that
the ratepayers of these two premises had accepted a 10% reduction in
their respective RVs. Their revised RV were set as follows –

23. Mrs Harris explained that the rateable value of a retail property was based
on the rental value for the property. Irrespective as to the nature of its
occupation, the property had to be valued as if it were vacant and to let.
The subject property is described as a café and premises and valued on a

Non-Domestic Rating Appeal

Page 5 of 8
shop basis by reference to the zoning method of valuation. Mrs Harris said
that this was the standard method of measuring retail premises to
calculate and compare their value.

24. Mrs Harris said that in order to determine the impact of the roadworks the
VO took into account the severity and duration of the disturbance as well
as trading information provided by ratepayer. She explained that two
identical properties in the same location would have had the same rent
when available to let although one business may suffer a greater loss due
to the disturbance of roadworks even though the rent for that property is
the same as that for the other. Mrs Harris said that an analysis of trade on
properties affected by the disturbance helped one determine what level of
allowance should be given. With reference to appeals which were made by
the ratepayers of neighbouring properties and following an inspection of
the area on 22nd March, the VO concluded that the works that affected the
properties in this location subsisted for approximately 13 weeks.

25. The roadworks completely closed the road junction and some pavements
around Church Street, Cresswell Street and St Georges Street from 2nd
January. The road outside properties in this vicinity were dug up by
Western Power up to 9th February 2018. After this, Pembrokeshire County
Council re-laid the whole surface moving along St George’s Street towards
Lower Frog Street and The Arches. The works consisted of two contiguous
schemes and were directly outside the property for approximately 13
weeks. The bulk of the work was completed in the third week of March
2018. Some work was re-done and machines were parked outside the
appeal property whilst the works moved up the road towards Lower Frog
Street. With reference to photographs taken on 22nd March 2018, Mrs
Harris pointed out that the works had been completed at that point.
Another photograph taken on the same day depicted the works moving
along St George Street and away from the appeal property.

26. Mrs Harris said that a rent of £25,000 pa was paid on the property and that
the landlord had not offered the tenant a concession during the duration of
the works. However, she reminded the Tribunal that the VO must assume
a hypothetical situation in which a reasonable landlord would be prepared
to accept part of any loss rather than lose a tenant. In such a scenario the
hypothetical landlord would reduce the rent in order to reflect the
disturbance caused by roadworks.

27. With reference to her Appendix 2; these contained details of the
appellant’s trade for the period 7th January 2018 to 25th March 2018 which,
if compared with the corresponding period in 2017, showed that trade had
diminished by some 9.45%. Mrs Harris said that if  one accepted that the
landlord might be prepared to accept part of any loss, she estimated a
reduction in RV would equate to 5%. However, the VO had to give a
considered view of the impact of disruption to all affected occupiers rather
than to just the appellant ratepayer by virtue of the use she had put to the
premises. In the case under consideration, Mrs Harris proposed an end
allowance, which was accepted by other neighbouring ratepayers, of 10%.

Non-Domestic Rating Appeal

Page 6 of 8

28. Since the nature of the road works was temporary, Mrs Harris asked the
Tribunal to make an order in under Regulation 34 (6) of the Non-Domestic
Rating (Alteration of Lists and Appeals) (Wales) Regulations 2005, as
amended. In this regulation stated –

Where it appears that circumstances giving rise to an alteration
ordered by a valuation tribunal have at the date of the decision ceased
to exist, the order may require the alteration to be made in respect of
such period as appears to the tribunal to be commensurate with the
duration of those circumstances.

29. In light of this Mrs Harris asked the Tribunal to confirm a revised list entry
of RV £16,000 with effect from 2nd January 2018 until 1st April 2018.

30. At the conclusion of the evidence the Tribunal decided to reserve its
decision.

Decision of the Tribunal

31. Having considered all of the evidence placed before it, the Tribunal
decided to allow the appeal to the extent Mrs Harris had conceded in her
evidence. The reasons for this were set out as follows -

32. When arriving at its decision, the Tribunal was governed by the rating
legislation laid down by Parliament.  Section 1(2) of the Rating (Valuation)
Act 1999 which amends paragraph 2(1) of Schedule 6 of The Local
Government Finance Act 1988 required that the rateable value of a
property is the amount that the hypothetical tenant coming fresh to the
scene would pay in rent on an annual basis assuming that the tenancy
began on the material day and that the property was put into reasonable
repair prior to the tenancy beginning, excluding any repairs that the
hypothetical landlord would consider uneconomic.  It is assumed that the
tenancy would have a reasonable prospect of continuance and that the
tenant would be responsible for all repairs and insuring the property.
Moreover, in rating, all hereditaments must be assumed to be vacant and
available to let on the statutory terms of the hypothetical tenancy.

33. The property and its locality must be considered as they physically existed
at the material day but at the level of rental values and in the economic
climate that existed as at the antecedent valuation date (AVD).  The AVD
was set by the Rating Lists (Valuation Date) (Wales) Order 2014  –

1st April 2015 is specified as the day by reference to which the rateable
values of nondomestic hereditaments are to be determined for the
purposes of local and central non-domestic rating lists which are
compiled for Wales on 1st April 2017.

34. The scope of this proposal only addressed the disruption caused by
roadworks situated within the vicinity of the subject property for the period

Non-Domestic Rating Appeal

Page 7 of 8
2nd January 2018 to 1st April 2018. The scope of the proposal could not be
extended to consider matters that subsequently occurred later in the year.
Whilst Mrs Harris had accepted that the road works had lasted long
enough and were sufficiently severe that the hypothetical landlord would
accept a lower annual rent, the question the Tribunal had to address was
had the appellant justified a further reduction beyond that conceded by
Mrs Harris in her revised valuation.

35. The Tribunal found nothing inherently wrong with Mrs Harris’ process
which involved looking at the scheme of works, considering its duration
and severity and, with reference to other forms of evidence such as the
previous year’s trade for the corresponding period, deduced that an end
allowance of 10% was fair and reasonable. This level of end allowance
was offered to and accepted by other occupiers in the vicinity, irrespective
as to whether they traded or not. The fact that a company did not trade
during the works did not mean that traders who did gained more of an end
allowance. Whilst the Tribunal also appreciated that trade gained from
regular customers might be lost, it considered that the reduction offered in
Mrs Harris’ valuation adequately reflected the temporary loss in trade.
There could be no compensation to reflect lost custom per se or to reflect
the time for that trade to return.

36. The Tribunal did not consider that the council’s failure to remove plant and
machinery away from the street at weekends added to the appellant’s
contention for a further reduction in her property’s RV. If the local authority
had promised to move equipment on the weekends but did not, then
redress for this, if there was any, lay elsewhere.

37. Whilst the Tribunal understood that works prevailed throughout parts of the
town, it was evident from the photographs supplied by Mrs Harris that
there were no works outside the appeal property by 22nd March. The
photographs showed that the works had gradually progressed along St
Georges Street towards the junction with Lower Frog Street.

38. The Tribunal attached no weight to the fact that a different end allowance
was given for a longer period in respect of disruption caused to business in
2012- 13. The appeal under consideration was made against an entry in
the 2017 Rating List whereas the issues referred to by Mrs Uka above
reflected circumstances which occurred during the life of the 2010 list.

39. The Tribunal noted that this case had been adjourned from a hearing
scheduled earlier in 2019 and understood Mrs Uka’s frustration of having
to attend a subsequent hearing at her own expense. However, the
Tribunal was not empowered to award costs to a party either by way of
compensation or in the event of their success at the hearing.

40. In its conclusion, the Tribunal did not believe that Mrs Uka’s case for a
reduction beyond that offered by Mrs Harris was justified for the reasons
given above. As a corollary, the Tribunal found by the facts presented that
the appeal property’s Rateable Value should be reduced to £16,0000 with

Non-Domestic Rating Appeal

Page 8 of 8
effect from 2nd January 2018 until 1st April 2018 and orders the Valuation
Officer for Wales to alter the Rating List to accord with its decision.

property: The Lounge 2, St Georges Street, Tenby, SA70 7JB
